justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing level of the S&P 500 at the time of the forecast, which was trading in the roughly 415–420 range. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, adding only a slight positive drift consistent with the long-run daily expected return of equities, which is negligibly small over a single session. For the one-week estimate, I maintained a similarly modest upward bias, reflecting the historical tendency of equities to grind higher in the absence of major shocks. For the one-month estimate, I allowed a slightly larger drift, consistent with annualized long-run equity returns of roughly 7–10%, prorated to a monthly figure. None of these point estimates embed a strong directional view; they are largely mean-drift projections from the anchor price.

The confidence interval widths reflect standard realized volatility assumptions for the S&P 500. At the one-day horizon, historical daily volatility runs around 1–1.5%, which translates to a relatively tight band. As the horizon extends to one week and then one month, uncertainty compounds roughly with the square root of time, which is why the one-month interval is substantially wider than the one-day interval. I also gave some additional weight to the macro environment at the time, which included elevated uncertainty around Federal Reserve policy, credit conditions, and slowing economic data, all of which argue for slightly wider-than-average intervals compared to a calm, low-volatility baseline.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a sudden shift in Federal Reserve communication, such as an unexpected rate hike or a sharp pivot in forward guidance, which could move markets several percent in a single session. A significant deterioration in credit markets, a geopolitical escalation, or an unexpected earnings shock from a large-cap constituent could similarly produce tail moves. On the upside, a surprisingly strong economic data print, a dovish Fed surprise, or a resolution of a major macro overhang could push the index above the upper bound of my intervals, particularly at the one-month horizon. These are low-probability but plausible scenarios that formal volatility models tend to underweight.

Finally, it is worth noting that my intervals are not immune to structural breaks. If something like a financial system stress event, a sudden liquidity crisis, or a geopolitical shock of unusual severity were to materialize, the realized outcome could fall well outside even my one-month 90% confidence interval. History shows that tail events in equity markets occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest, and my intervals should be understood as a reasonable central range rather than a guarantee that extreme outcomes are impossible.
